content: 1. Proton pump inhibitors were analyzed within the context of a state employee health plan, as discussed in the Journal of Managed Care Pharmacy in 2020. 2. Stargardt, Schreyögg, and Busse explored fixed drug pricing in Germany, focusing on group formation, price calculation using regression methods, and the effects of these policies, as published in Gesundheitswesen in 2005. 3. Marđetko and Kos examined the introduction of therapeutic reference pricing in Slovenia and its economic consequences, as detailed in the European Journal of Health Economics in 2018. 4. Stargardt investigated the impact of reference pricing on switching behavior and healthcare utilization, specifically in the case of statins in Germany, published in the European Journal of Health Economics in 2010. 5. Armeni, Jommi, and Otto analyzed the simultaneous effects of pharmaceutical policies from the perspectives of payers and patients, using Italy as a case study, as published in the European Journal of Health Economics in 2016. 6. Schneeweiss et al. evaluated the net health plan savings from reference pricing for angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors among elderly residents in British Columbia, as published in Medical Care in 2004. 7. Andersson et al. assessed the effects of policy changes in Sweden’s pharmaceutical reimbursement schedule on drug expenditures, using interrupted time series analysis, as published in Health Policy in 2006. 8. Leopold et al. studied the impact of pharmaceutical policy interventions on the utilization of antipsychotic medicines in Finland and Portugal during economic recessions, as published in the International Journal for Equity in Health in 2014. 9. Von der Schulenburg, Vandoros, and Kanavos reviewed the effects of drug market regulation on pharmaceutical prices in Europe, with a focus on ACE inhibitors, as published in the Health Economics Review in 2020. 10. Grootendorst et al. analyzed the impact of reference pricing for nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents on the use and costs of analgesic drugs, as published in Health Services Research in 2005. 11. The World Health Organization (WHO) provided definitions and guidelines on health technology assessment, emphasizing its importance in decision-making processes, as accessed in 2020. 12. Ben-Aharon, Shavit, and Magnezi examined whether drug price regulation affects healthcare expenditures, as published in the European Journal of Health Economics in 2017. 13. Kwon et al. analyzed the effects of price cuts on drug spending in South Korea, focusing on antihyperlipidemic agents, as published in Health Policy in 2020. 14. Harris critiqued discriminatory practices in healthcare decision-making, as discussed in the Journal of Medical Ethics in 2005. 15. Nord, Daniels, and Kamlet addressed challenges associated with quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) in healthcare evaluations, as published in Value in Health in 2009. 16. Caro et al. debated the determination of value in health technology assessment, as published in Pharmacoeconomics in 2018. 17. Rajan, Gutierrez-Ibarluzea, and Moharra explored issues in promoting health technology assessment, including motives, enablers, and barriers, as published in the International Journal of Technology Assessment in Health Care in 2011. 18. Abdel Rida et al. conducted a systematic review of pharmaceutical pricing policies in developing countries, as published in the Journal of Pharmaceutical Health Services Research in 2017. 19. The WHO Collaborating Centre for Pharmaceutical Pricing and Reimbursement Policies provided insights into pharmaceutical pricing and reimbursement challenges beyond financial crises, as presented at the 2015 PPRI Conference. 20. Cheng et al. studied the effects of the zero mark-up policy on medicines in Beijing community health facilities, as published in Pharmaceutical Policy and Law in 2012. 21. Fu, Li, and Yip analyzed the intended and unintended impacts of price changes for drugs and medical services in China, as published in Social Science & Medicine in 2020. 22. Yang et al. evaluated the impact of the zero-markup drug policy on hospitalization expenditures in rural China, as published in Tropical Medicine & International Health in 2017. 23. Zhou et al. assessed the financial impact of the zero-markup policy for essential drugs on patients in county hospitals in rural China, as published in PLOS One in 2015. 24. Li et al. evaluated the effects of implementing the zero-markup policy in community health service institutions in Chengdu, as published in the Chinese Journal of New Drugs in 2008. 25. Bhaskarabhatla et al. examined the regulatory impact of partial price controls on metformin in India, as published in Health Policy and Planning in 2017. 26. Lu et al. analyzed changes in the use of antidiabetic medications following price regulations in China, as published in the Journal of Pharmaceutical Health Services Research in 2013. 27. Chu, Liu, and Romeis assessed the effects of drug price reduction policies on older populations in Taiwan, as published in Health Services Management Research in 2011. 28. The WHO emphasized the importance of improving transparency in markets for medicines, vaccines, and other health products, as discussed during the 72nd World Health Assembly in 2019. 29. Kohler et al. examined the role of pharmaceutical pricing transparency in Brazil’s public procurement system, as published in Global Health in 2015. 30. Moodley and Suleman evaluated the impact of South Africa’s single exit price policy on originator and generic medicines, as published in BMC Health Services Research in 2019. 31. 32. Pauwels et al. reviewed managed entry agreements for oncology drugs in Europe, as published in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2017. 33. Langley et al. evaluated the impact of price transparency interventions on institutional expenditures for commonly prescribed medications, as published in the Future Healthcare Journal in 2018. 34. Berdud et al. discussed the future of global health procurement and issues surrounding pricing transparency, as published in 2020. 35. Moon advocated for removing opacity in medicine pricing, as published in the British Medical Journal in 2020. 36. Clark, Heltzer, and Rankin provided guidance on managing the tender process for medicines, as discussed in the MDS-3 Managing Access to Medicines and Technologies manual. 37. Maniadakis et al. explored strategies for shaping pharmaceutical tenders to enhance effectiveness and sustainability in countries with expanding healthcare coverage, as published in Applied Health Economics and Health Policy in 2018. 38. Garattini, Van de Vooren, and Freemantle analyzed value-based pricing and tendering for HPV vaccines in Italy, as published in the Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine in 2014. 39. Adesina, Wirtz, and Dratler reviewed Mexico’s experience with reforming antiretroviral price negotiations and public procurement, as published in Health Policy and Planning in 2013. 40. Wouters et al. assessed the impact of pharmaceutical tendering on prices and market concentration in South Africa over a 14-year period, as published in Social Science & Medicine in 2020. 41. The WHO provided operational principles for good pharmaceutical procurement, emphasizing best practices for ensuring cost-effectiveness and sustainability. 42. Kaplan et al. outlined policy options for promoting the use of generic medicines in lowand middle-income countries, as published in 2020. 43. Rémuzat et al. provided an overview of supply-side and demand-side policies for biosimilars in 10 European member states, as published in the Journal of Market Access & Health Policy in 2020. 44. The Center for Drug Evaluation and Research issued guidance on clinical immunogenicity considerations for biosimilar and interchangeable insulin products. 45. Buzzelli et al. analyzed the impact of generic substitution on pharmaceutical prices and expenditures in OECD countries, as published in the Journal of Pharmaceutical Finance, Economics & Policy in 2006. 46. Andersson et al. evaluated the effects of generic substitution reforms on patients’ and society’s pharmaceutical expenditures in Sweden, as published in Health Policy in 2007. 47. Clark et al. assessed the cost savings and increased adherence associated with an employer value-based benefits program targeting generic antihyperlipidemic and antidiabetic medications, as published in Journal of Managed Care Pharmacy in 2014. 48. Fraeyman et al. examined the evolution of co-payment and generic market share for common medications in Belgium’s reference pricing system, as published in Applied Health Economics and Health Policy in 2013. 49. Chen et al. analyzed the effects of Taiwan’s generic grouping price policy on drug prices and expenditures, focusing on cardiovascular drugs, as published in BMC Public Health in 2008. 50. Godman et al. reviewed initiatives in Sweden to enhance ARB prescribing efficiency following generic losartan availability, as published in the International Journal of Clinical Practice in 2013. 51. Lee et al. evaluated the success of Argentina’s generic drug law, as published in Value in Health in 2013. 52. Bhargava et al. assessed the impact of adding generic medication vouchers to a pharmacist academic detailing program on generic dispensing ratios, as published in Journal of Managed Care Pharmacy in 2010. 53. Danzon and Furukawa provided cross-national evidence on generic pharmaceuticals in pharmacyversus physician-driven markets, as published in an NBER Working Paper. 54. Balmaceda et al. analyzed the impact of therapeutic equivalence policies on medicine prices in Chile, as published in Value in Health Regional Issues in 2020. 55. Colgan et al. conducted a systematic review of perceptions of generic medications among the general population, doctors, and pharmacists, as published in BMJ Open in 2015. 56. Gebresillassie et al. evaluated perceptions and concerns regarding generic medicines among patients, physicians, and pharmacy professionals in Gondar, Ethiopia, as published in PLOS One in 2018. 57. Jacobs et al. conducted an international survey on patient attitudes and understanding of biosimilars, as published in Patient Preference and Adherence in 2016. 58. The WHO provided guidelines on registration requirements for multisource (generic) pharmaceutical products to establish interchangeability. 59. The WHO issued guidelines on evaluating monoclonal antibodies as similar biotherapeutic products (SBPs). 60. The WHO provided guidelines on the quality, safety, and efficacy of biotherapeutic protein products prepared using recombinant DNA technology. 61. Ferraresi et al. examined whether centralized purchasing reduces public expenditure in the Italian healthcare system, as published in Social Italiana di Economia Pubblica in 2017. 62. Toulemon analyzed the effects of group purchasing on hospital medicine prices, as published in Health Economics in 2018. 63. Baldi and Vannoni studied the impact of centralization on pharmaceutical procurement prices, focusing on institutional quality and corruption, as published in Regional Studies in 2017. 64. Dubois et al. explored pooled procurement of drugs in lowand middle-income countries. 65. Kim and Skordis-Worrall assessed whether voluntary pooled procurement could reduce the price of antiretroviral drugs, using Efavirenz as a case study, as published in Health Policy and Planning in 2017. 66. Barbosa and Fiuza analyzed demand aggregation and credit risk effects in pooled procurement in Brazil’s public pharmaceutical purchases. 67. The WHO provided insights into multi-country regional pooled procurement of medicines. 68. The Australian Government Department of Health outlined procedures for setting approved ex-manufacturer prices for new or extended pharmaceutical listings. 69. Mamiya provided an update on Japan’s drug pricing system. 70. Véran discussed Amendment No. 474, related to pharmaceutical pricing in France. 71. The WHO examined the trade of pharmaceutical products and its implications. 72. Bauer analyzed the compounding effects of tariffs on medicines, estimating the real cost of protectionism in emerging markets. 73. Creese discussed the impact of sales taxes on medicines in a working paper.
